definitions.text: Scared = a stock whose TET mood reading sits in its washed-out zone. Fear % = how deep it sits, 0–100; above 50% = scared.
How rare = the share of the stock's own days since 2013 (or since its history starts, if later) that were this scared or worse, counting only days before today.

Peers = the other stocks on the board in its industry (otherwise its sector, otherwise the whole board), or its AI, Semis or Neocloud crowd when that crowd is more scared. Peer gap = its fear % minus the fear % of the middle stock of its peers (a calm stock reads 0%), in points.
Outlier score 0–100: highest when the fear is rare for the stock itself and its peers are calm; lower when the stock is often this scared, or when its peers are just as scared.

Alone = few of its peers are scared. With the crowd = most of its peers are scared too. Deep = scared on daily, weekly, 2-week and monthly candles. Rare = this scared on 1% of its own days or fewer. Fast = one of its fastest 5-day drops in mood.

On the board: stocks of the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, Russell 1000 and Russell 2000 with enough price, trading and history and a bar for the latest session. Left out: funds, stocks held flat by a cash deal, one-day jumps that volume does not back, unadjusted spin-off drops and the less-traded share class of a company with two.

Crowds = 11 sectors, 4 indexes, 4 themes (AI, Semis, High beta, Neocloud) and the industries with enough stocks on the board. Industries come from the SEC's industry codes (SIC), grouped into plain crowds, plus four hand-built ones (space, nuclear & uranium, oilfield services & drilling, energy shipping); a stock without a code is compared with its sector. Today's index lists are carried back in time.
Alarm line = a high reading for that candle size by the crowd's own history; the S&P 500's is the Fear meter's.

defs.text: Business = the 200W business score, 0–100: growth, cash-flow and valuation numbers, each ranked against the S&P 500 + Nasdaq 100. 70+ strong, 50–69 middling, under 50 weak; — = no score. A crowd shows the median of its scored stocks.
